utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Jordash, the Chamber was informed that you would like to raise a matter. I don't know whether it should be done in private session or in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Open session is okay, I think, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's a very straightforward issue. It's a request for a more detailed medical note from Dr. Eekhof. And the reason for the request is that I've observed, at least, that the court schedule is challenging for Mr. Stanisic and he certainly is exhausted after hearings and exhausted during the days that we do not sit. Now, I don't know if that's medically significant or not and I make to pretense that I can assess that, and I equally do not suggest that Mr. Stanisic is saying at this stage that he cannot cope, but certainly he has noticed the effects of the court schedule. And for the -- out of abundance of caution, I would respectfully request that Dr. Eekhof at least address whether the tiredness, whether the fatigue, whether the increase in difficult symptoms is medically significant or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, it's -- we'll pay attention to it. We'll think about it and we'll see what -- how to phrase the additional questions for Dr. Eekhof if we would decide that we would put additional questions to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, what you told us -- of course, if we read the regular reports, you see that sometimes there are small fluctuations. Although they're relatively steady, it's not always the same. I noticed that you approach the matter in a rather broad way and not saying especially his left leg causes him more concerns the last week or, I mean, so we'll deal with the matter in the way you approached it and that's what we'll orient ourselves upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I perhaps add this: that Mr. Stanisic takes pain relief, and what I've mainly observed is that he's taking more of that pain relief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a very concrete matter which we could include if we put any additional questions to Dr. Eekhof. Yes. Any other specific matter? Apart from feeling exhausted, apparently it's your suggestion that there may be a medically significant extra burden upon him at this moment which exhausts him. That's -- the pain relief, of course, is a very concrete aspect. Is there any other such concrete element which you could mention so that we don't forget to specifically address that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think it's the pain relief which is significant because, as you know, Mr. Stanisic has a number of complaints and sometimes the pain emanates from one and not the other and the next day it's changed. What we would find useful is a comment on why there has been or if there has been an increase, and, two, whether in fact that pain relief affects Mr. Stanisic's ability to concentrate, because some of that pain relief from a layperson's point of view is medication which one wouldn't want to take on too regular a basis. And I particularly refer to morphine which Mr. Stanisic takes on occasion. I think that's when the pain is particularly significant. And as I say, from a layperson's point of view, morphine sounds relatively serious, and relatively serious in the sense of being able to focus and concentrate on complex court proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you say apart from pain relief it may have side effects.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I just asked you to be as concrete as possible so that we would not overlook any matter when considering your request. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Just to request that we would have an opportunity to propose some questions as well that we also have for the doctor, with the Chamber's leave of course. We could do that in whatever format Your Honour sees fit. We can do it by e-mail informally, in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider in which format, if any questions are put to Dr. Eekhof, and what format that would be done and whether we would consult the parties. Of course we've heard from Mr. Jordash what his concerns are and why he would like to ask a more thorough report on Dr. Eekhof. If you have similar suggestions or questions, then I think the earlier it comes to the Chamber ... I can even imagine that you put one or two or three things on paper, send an e-mail, copy the Chamber on it so that Mr. Jordash is informed, and we would then -- we would be able to consider whether to include it, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: We will do that, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then a few other matters, not too much. Mr. Jordash, I think that you still owe us further information in relation to D56. That's what you promised more or less, I think, yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I do. And if Your Honours would just indulge us a little until the break and then I will obtain what information there is. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll wait for that. Then finally the other matter is, Mr. Jordash, the Stanisic Defence was granted leave on the 4th of July to reply to the Prosecution's response to the Defence motion for admission of 92 ter material for Witness DST-035. I think that we have not seen anything, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think that's absolutely right, and I apologise for that also. And we can put together a reply by tomorrow because it goes to, in substance, what was in the application to reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you would be out of the time-limit, wouldn't you, I mean, to do it tomorrow? Rule 126 bis: Unless otherwise ordered, a motion filed by a party shall be filed within 14 days -- a response be filed within 14 days. A reply to the response, if any, shall be filed within seven days of the filing of the response, with the leave of the relevant Chamber. So the time-limit is set in general terms there. Leave has been granted on the 4th of July, and let's not argue about whether we should start counting from the 4th or whether we should start counting from the 29th of June when the response was filed. In both cases we are beyond the seven days.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I can only apologise, it was an administrative oversight, and request that Your Honours ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So perhaps if you want to file something tomorrow, then perhaps it would be good to address also the late filing and that you perhaps ask - I'm not in any way anticipating on what a decision would be - but to -- I even add to that, if you want to have a longer time-limit, that usually you should ask that within the time available to respond and not to do it afterwards. But I leave it in your hands. But just to bring to your attention that there may well be a problem and we'll see what you do with it and then you'll see what we are going to do with it. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These were the matters I wanted to draw the attention of the parties to. Next witness, Mr. Jordash, without protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Without protective measures, Mr. Bosnic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bosnic. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration of which the text will now be handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Bosnic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bosnic, I think it should be made a tiny little bit shorter, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now it's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bosnic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Jordash. Mr. Jordash is counsel for Mr. Stanisic. Mr. Jordash, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bosnic.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could you state your full name and date of birth for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Mile Bosnic, son of Milivoj, born on the 30th of October, 1958, in Virovitica, Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And your ethnic origin is?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now could we have on the screen, please, 1D4902.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What's going to come up on the screen in front of you, Mr. Bosnic, is a statement. Would you have a look at the front of the statement, and do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you interviewed on the 21st of September, 2006; 17th and 20th of May, 2011; 1st of June, 2011?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If we just go to the next page of the statement, just to ensure that you recognise this. Do you recall giving this statement to the Stanisic Defence on the dates which we've just discussed?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes, and you can see my signature, my last name, with which I initialled the pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you had an opportunity prior to attending court today to carefully review this statement?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we please have on the screen 1D4914. Sorry, no, 1D4916.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When you reviewed this statement which we've just seen on the screen, did you make any amendments to that statement on the 8th of July, 2011?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: The text is in English, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me just see if there is B/C/S, Mr. Bosnic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It apparently is not in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Apparently there is no B/C/S so we'll have to go through them orally. Do you recall making amendments to your statement on the 8th of July, Mr. Bosnic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, is there a B/C/S version anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, apparently not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Have we checked whether the witness reads any English?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm fairly sure he doesn't, but I'll ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you read any English, Mr. Bosnic?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Well, no, I can't. I don't understand English. I can skim through the text. I do know that I supplemented the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's see whether we can find a -- you said you supplemented the statement. Have you ever seen or was the result of your amendments ever discussed with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I was present and dictated these amendments myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I do not know to what extent every single amendment is relevant now already for your examination-in-chief. Is there any way that, for example, with someone -- you may have someone available who could translate the amendments to him so that the witness can report to us, for example, after the first break, that what was translated to him is -- reflects the amendments he wished to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's -- I think we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, of course, if there's any paragraph changed on which you would like to specifically deal with certain matters, then of course you would have to deal with those amendments immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. I think we can proceed as Your Honour suggests. And if there is a problem, then I'll deal with the amendment orally, but I don't think there will be. And the amendments are not in the main critical to his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I'd like that to be done if possible during the first break so that the Prosecution is not later suffering from any challenge to the amendments that are put on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We'll return to this later on, Mr. Bosnic. Let's now turn to 1D4914.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry to interrupt. I was just waiting to see what was going to be pulled up. With respect to the 92 ter statement, the 92 ter filing included the draft English version, unsigned and undated, if I'm not mistaken, with draft on top not reviewed by witness and not signed. But the B/C/S version was signed in the motion. So I just would like it to be clarified, and that's why I'm mentioning it now, when we turn back to the amendments, whether the amendments were made into the B/C/S version; so does the B/C/S version differ from the English version or is the B/C/S signed version identical to the English unsigned version? In other words, we'd like to know which version incorporates the proofing note of 8th July and, et cetera, we'd like to know which version is what. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Both the B/C/S statement and the English statement are the same. The amendments which were made with reference to the B/C/S statement were put into this chart, so the English and the B/C/S statement are the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you recall, Mr. Bosnic, being shown a number of exhibits or documents and being asked to go through them and make your comments in a chart?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If we can go to the bottom of the page of the chart. A bit further, please, so we can see the initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you recognise the initials?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. And do you recognise the chart and the documents discussed or the documents listed on the left column and the comments on the right?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to review your comments before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And did you make any clarifications or corrections that you wish to make?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the comments that you made, did they accord with the truth?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May this chart be tendered as an exhibit, Your Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I suggest that the -- that the 92 ter statement will be MFI'd for the time being because it may still be subject to amendments, and the same would be done for the proofing notes. And, Ms. Marcus, any objection against admission of the chart, the chart which gives the comments of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar, first, the 92 ter statement would receive number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number D313, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D313 is marked for identification. The proofing notes ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D314, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- is marked for identification. And then the chart containing comments of the witness on various documents ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D315, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D315 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, let me take you -- well, before I do that, what is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: I have a degree in political science.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, let me take you to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, a degree is as far -- is not an occupation but is a title. What is the present occupation of the witness; that question has not been answered. Could you tell us what your occupation is at this moment. Do you have a job, are you ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am unemployed at present. I was supposed to attend an interview, a job interview, just before coming here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was your last job, could you tell us, when and what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 2001 I was employed in the commodity reserves in Banja Luka, commodity reserves of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you stayed in that job until ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Roughly a year. A year and ten months. Or, my apologies, what I meant was a year and roughly ten days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Briefly, where were you born and where did you grow up?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: I was born in Virovitica and I grew up in Podravska Slatina, where I completed my secondary education. It's a small town in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And in 1990 where did you live?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: In Velika Kladusa, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And as we can see from your statement you were politically active during the -- before and during the war in Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, to assist the Trial Chamber, I want to ask you to look at a map and indicate on the map the locations where you were politically active so that the Trial Chamber can see where your evidence is going to encompass or what your evidence is going to encompass.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have P258. And could Mr. Bosnic be given a pen so that he can draw on the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's very small.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It can be enlarged.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we go to page 2, perhaps that's the best way. I think that might be a more appropriate map. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Would you indicate, please -- perhaps I can give you some guidance here. First, Slunj.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Velika Kladusa.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Petrinja.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Pakrac.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: I was not in Pakrac in 1991 but later, but I can mark it nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Mark it then, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Plitvice, please. Plitvice.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: We don't have Plitvice depicted here but there are between Slunj and Korenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Knin.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Vojnic.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Vrginmost.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Petrova Gora.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Petrova Gora is between Vojnic and Vrginmost; it's a mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Golubic.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: It is somewhere on the way out of Knin in the direction of Grahovo and the village of Strmica. I can't tell, really, but roughly here. I can't give you the exact location. At any rate, it's on the way out of Knin in the direction of Bosnia-Herzegovina, specifically Grahovo and the village of Strmica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Glina.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Veljun.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: It is on the territory of the municipality of Slunj. We don't have it depicted. It's somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Plaski.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Plaski is between Slunj and Ogulin. Roughly here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And Bruska.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Bruska is somewhere near Benkovac. I was there, but I can't give you the exact location.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Bosnic, would you like to adjust your headphones? It's a long afternoon to be holding your headphones.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to. I'm doing my best, but I keep taking my glasses off so I -- I'll be able to adjust them on occasion, no problem there, but I do hear everything you say. If I don't, I'll let you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I tender this as an exhibit. I don't know if it's assisted Your Honours at all, but I hope it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think the most practical way would have been to prepare such a map, to agree with the Prosecution where the places are, and then to give it. That takes -- instead of six or seven minutes, takes half a minute. And apart from that, of course, some of these locations may be well known. But that might be different for various judges. But it's typically a matter on which you could easily agree, I think, where Slunj is and where Petrova Gora is. So that would have been more practical, but ... No objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the marked map would receive number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number D316, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D316 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we please have D313, your statement, on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, let's go to paragraph 2. This statement is now before the Court, Mr. Bosnic, and I want to ask you to elaborate on some aspects of it. Paragraph 2 is where you discuss becoming politically active from the end of May 1990. You established a local SDS board in Kordun. Was this the only local SDS board being formed at the time or was this part of a process?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: At the time, it was the only SDS board in Kordun.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And other places within Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes, mainly in Lika and Northern Dalmatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what was the process by which the local SDS board was formed?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: The Serbs in other areas except for Lika and Northern Dalmatia voted for Racan's party, the Alliance of Communists of Croatia, the Social Democratic Party, because that party accepted the constitutional status of the Serb people and agreed to Croatia remaining in the federal union. That's why most of the Serbs voted at the elections for Ivica Racan's party, and it was, in fact, 21 Serbs who became MPs on his ticket. However, subsequently when this party agreed to the policy pushing for Croatia's independence, that was when SDS boards started being set up across Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what was the political agenda of the SDS in May of 1990 and subsequently when other municipalities began to arrange SDS boards?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: The key issue of the SDS political agenda was that should Croatia remain in Yugoslavia, we would agree to a certain degree of autonomy within Croatia. However, if Croatia decides to withdraw from Yugoslavia, we, as the second largest constituent people in Croatia, express our desire to remain within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: At what stage or at what point in time did you first meet Milan Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: I first met Milan Babic before a rally of the SDS held in a place called Srb in July of 1990. That was when I met him in person. But I apologise, I do have to mention the fact that we were together attending a number of meetings as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Before you met him in Srb in July of 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes. I attended meetings that he too attended, but we didn't have a direct contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And in which capacity were you attending those meetings and in which capacity was he?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: I attended them as a member of the SDS Main Board. Every representative of a newly-established local board became a member of the Main Board, and Babic by that time was already a member of the Main Board. I think he was in fact vice-president of the party or the president of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So the Main Board of the SDS consisted of the leaders of the local boards, and you just mention now that Babic was, you thought, may be the vice-president of the party, you mean the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the Executive Board was what?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: The Executive Board was the executive body of the Main Board. It operated in the field in networking various local boards and preparing the material to be discussed by the Main Board. In other words, it was an executive body of the Main Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And by the time you met Babic in July of 1990, what was Babic's position, can you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: He was the mayor. In other words, the president of the municipality of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what position did he told in the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: He was one of the five leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what position, if any, did he occupy in the Executive Board of the Main Board?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: I think he was president.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the other four leaders of the SDS party were whom?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: The disputable leader at that moment was Professor Raskovic. Then Zelenbaba, Jovo Opacic. I cannot recall the other names, but there were 19 founders, some of whom were already mayors, were presidents of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And during 1990, having met Babic in July of 1990, how many times and in which circumstances were you meeting Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: There were many instances. The meetings of the Main Board were held every seven or 15 days, depending on the development of the situation in the field and depending on the actual needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And did you have a role within the Main Board other than attending as a leader of a local board?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: I was just a member of the Main Board, but I was also in charge for the area -- of the area from which I came within the Main Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How many members were in the Main Board?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: The number changed, but 150, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And as a member of a local board attending the Main Board, function did you play? What did you do when you attended? What happened at the meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: We discussed further policy moves of the party. First of all, what would be done, what would be the course of action where the SDS was already in power, in those places; and secondly, what was to be specifically done in order for the SDS to take over power in those municipalities where it was not in power.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was there a voting process?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what was the nature of the voting process?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: It would be a show of hands. And if a decision was adopted by the majority, it would be a binding decision upon the leadership of the SDS as well as upon the local authorities, i.e., the mayors, of course depending on the nature of the specific decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was there any circumstances where there wasn't a need for a majority, where one person or a group of people could outvote the majority?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were circumstances, and this did happen occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can you give an example, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: For instance, when there was a difference of opinions as to whether to go to the elections in Serbia or not, Professor Raskovic was in favour of the SDS being part of the elections in Serbia, and Professor Raskovic was outvoted. In fact, he, Zelenbaba, and Jovo Opacic walked out of the decision at a certain point and this led to strife in the party and the leaving of the party by the two last-mentioned gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But the question I asked was whether there were circumstances where the majority could be outvoted or whether, in fact, it was -- issues were always decided by majority voting.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge was there always majority voting or not?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: If you mean whether mistakes could have been made in the counting or if a problem could have arisen in connection with a counting, yes, that was possible because the hands were counted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Bosnic, it's probably me, but let me just try once more. When an issue went to the vote, how was it decided? Was it by majority voting or were there other ways in which an issue could be decided?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: I think that I already answered this. The proposition, the proposal, which received a majority of votes would be adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what kind of issues through 1990 were being decided by the Main Board?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: There were numerous issues and there were many problems in connection of the ways of protecting the Serbian population, in which way to strengthen the SDS and to take over power, also in the areas of Kordun and Banija, and to start building a political system in order to be able to parry the moves of Croatia and to set up organs in a broader area, the Lika and Northern Dalmatia area to begin with, and later also for Krajina. And we also discussed the question of village guards to protect against any dangers coming from the Croatian regime and a lot of other questions. I could go on at some length about those.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's fine for now. Could we return to your witness statement, D313 and paragraph 4. Paragraph 4 you discuss there an attack on Petrinja and the organisation of night guards. Did this -- in this paragraph, you note "the SDS only established local night guards to ensure nothing happened." What were local night guards? What did they do and where were they at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Local night guards consisted of the local villagers who stood guards in their villages during the night in order to prevent any attacks, Croatian attacks by their police units or by the National Guard. These were local people, villagers, peasants who, while standing guard, carried mainly their own weapons, mainly hunting weapons which were their weapons, in their possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: "Mainly hunting weapons which were their weapons, in their possession." Was there any other source of weapons at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: At that time, no. Later it became possible to buy weapons from smugglers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: At what point in time did it become possible to buy weapons from smugglers?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: We were already in October when incursions by special Croatian units started and when newly set up police stations were established in places where they had not been previously, which places were adjacent to Serbian villages. It was not -- it did not happen at the same time everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's just break that down a bit. Do you know where local night guards were approximately, how many of the villages, in October of 1990 and towards the end of 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: In all the villages in the Kordun area, and I went to see them. As regards the other areas, I cannot say with certainty, but the principle was the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was the setting up of the night guards in other areas, in all the areas covered by the SDS local boards, discussed at the Main Board?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, this came in October of 1990. But as your statement says at paragraph 9, barricades had already gone up in Knin on the 16th and 17th of August, 1990. Was that discussed at the SDS Main Board?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was, but after the erection of the barricades, because the events of the 16th, 17th, and the 18th were sudden. No one actually had expected that Croatian special units would seek to disarm the local police, the reserve force of the local police.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what form did the discussion take at the Main Board, this event having happened? Was there discussion about organising for future events?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: We were taken by surprise, very much so, and the key question is what course of action to take.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what was decided?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: The decision which was made was that we should try and find a solution which would make it possible for our own police to efficiently count the Croatian Special Police units and the National Guard units because it was evident that the local village guards with the armaments that they had just could not do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were decisions made by the Main Board? Practical decisions, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Not at that moment. At that moment we actually started discussing our further course of action and what measures to take.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And where did the creation of night guards come from? Where were the discussions -- sorry, when were the discussions? And was the decision to create night guards part of a number of decisions which were in response to the events?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: It was actually kind of an extorted reaction to the developments that were taking place, because the people started to self-organise in a number of villages. So in order to prevent incidents and undesirable situations, we thought that the SDS should place such guards under some form of control and to link all of them into a sort of a unified whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what was Milan Babic's role in this decision-making, if you recall it?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Milan Babic was the key figure in the adoption of all our decisions because being a man of -- an operative, he knew all of us were in the field, and we supported him and we always voted for his proposals and the decisions that he proposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But why was that, why did the Main Board place such trust with Milan Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: We trusted him because we thought that he was the one who most directly and most efficiently conveyed our positions and our opinions and translated them into proposals of decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what was your personal relationship with Milan Babic through the -- towards the end of 1990 and early 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: I can say that our relations were correct and as of October 1991 they were in fact exceptional. We were friends. And I thought myself one of his more intimate associates within the circle of five or six of his closest associates. With time, this friendship strengthened.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And before October 1991, during 1991 itself, how often would you see him, and, again, in which circumstances, generally? We'll come to the specifics shortly.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Very frequently, every seven or 15 days. There wouldn't be longer breaks than 15 days. We would go to Knin and he would attend our meetings in Kordun at Banija in October as well as later regarding the establishment of the Territorial Defence and the adoption of the Statute of the SAO Krajina in the Kordun municipalities. Simply, we were frequently in personal contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me ask you, please, about 65 ter 436.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's in Your Honours' chart at the beginning. Could we have it on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I want to ask you to elaborate on a number of things.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D302, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You've seen this before and you've commented on it; that's right, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, this is a statement, as we can see, from a Mr. Ognjen. And within the statement he discusses the Council of National Resistance. What was Babic's role within the Council of National Resistance in October of 19 -- sorry, in December of 1990, the date of this statement?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: In August.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The statement is dated December of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We can see -- we can go to the 5th page of the English and the 6th page of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The statement is December 1990. And since we are on the last page, you can see there, three paragraphs from the top, what the author of this statement is saying: "I also know that citizens were given the weapons of the Knin SJS reservists. These weapons were handed out on the 17th of August, 1990, after the Knin SJS warehouse was broken into, but I don't know exactly whom the weapons were issued to. I heard that there was a list stating to whom the weapons were given, and I know that in that period Dragan Batas of Strmica was in charge of 10 men who were guarding Milan Babic, Knin SO president, and that probably they had been issued some of the weapons." And then the second paragraph from the bottom: "I also want to mention that people in town are openly saying that Simo Dubajic and Milo Martic are handing out weapons and probably have lists of the people they sold the weapons to." You following me, Mr. Bosnic?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't have this in Serbia when you made this reference to Mr. Batas. As for Simo Dubajic and Martic, I have it in Serbian. But -- no, I apologise, I have found it. Now it's all right. I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Just a have a read of that to yourself.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes. All right. I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can you comment on that? Do you know anything about this in August of 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: The first time I heard that Milan Martic distributed any weapons, to the best of my knowledge he did not do that. There were different stories being bandied about. People were saying that Simo Dubajic was selling some rifles, but I don't know about that firsthand. But as for Martic, there were no such stories.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And who was Simo Dubajic?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Simo Dubajic was a fighter in the Second World War who was more of a Bohemian and less of a fighter, actually. He was long on talk and short on deeds.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. Let's just return to my question about the Council for National Resistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If we turn to page 1 of the English and 1 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The author says the following halfway down the English page: "I'm aware that after a state of war was declared, the staff for defence of Knin --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please provide the reference in the original and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Page 1 of the English and 1 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And where approximately?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In the B/C/S, it's about halfway down the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: "I am aware that a state of war was declared -- I am aware that after a state of war was declared, the staff for defence of Knin was formed in the Omladinsko Naselje settlement in the village of Golubic. The staff was later renamed Council of National Resistance." And then the author goes on to list a number of people associated with Council of National Resistance. And if we go over the page to -- are you following me, Mr. Bosnic?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm following. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Then towards the bottom of that page, the writer also says: "I learned that the staff members," with reference to the Council of National Resistance, "also included Zelenbaba, Opacic," over the page in the English, page 2 of the B/C/S, "Peric, and Milan Babic, Knin SO municipal president who was also staff commander. Martic was saying that he was given the duty of staff commander and they were all given their duties by Milan Babic to add a sense of seriousness to the work." Can you comment on what the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have a couple of objections. First of all, counsel is using this statement of a witness who didn't testify. This is generally something that we oppose. Now, I saw the comments - and it's something that counsel also opposes, I should add. It's an out-of-court statement, untested. Having read the comments of the witness in the comments chart, I hesitated to make that objection because I think that the content does relate, certainly in part at least, to the witness's knowledge. However, what counsel is now proceeding to do is to ask leading questions using quotations from this statement. So I would object to the way it's being used. I think the -- with respect to the admission of the statement, which counsel hasn't done yet but I presume he's going to tender it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're talking about D302, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is marked for identification. So therefore --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I was -- yes, I was talking about the -- the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the chart.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No, 65 ter 436, which is what we're ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that is D302. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I apologise for that, in that case. But I would like to maintain my objection that the way that the counsel is leading the witness is not by asking open-ended questions and then comparing it to the -- to what we have in front of us but, rather, by putting statements in a way which leads the witness to a particular answer. So I'd like to request open-ended questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I can do it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you proceed, we have a kind of a practice developed here that you not put a statement of another witness or a testimony of another witness to a witness unless you have asked specifically about the subject matter and only after that, if there's any need to do so, to put the statement or earlier testimony to the witness. And of course this is already our practice in cross-examination, so let alone in chief, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I would submit that that's not accurate. That there is a practice where statements of witnesses who have testified in this courtroom or whose statements have been admitted pursuant to Rule 66, that's the practice. But in relation to exhibits, in relation to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not an exhibit yet. I mean, D302 is marked for identification because I think it was -- that still has to be considered, what kind of a statement this is, and I think we are still waiting for objections to -- not to say that there will be objections, but at least that matter has not been settled yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't know the exhibit number off the top of my head, but the Prosecution produced, during a witness's testimony, a statement by Ilija Kojic given to the RS MUP in 2003 and used it to cross-examine a witness and then applied to have it admitted. And despite what my learned friend has just said, we didn't oppose that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't have a clear recollection of how that exactly was used. If statements are taken not for the purposes of this Tribunal, then at least 92 ter does not oppose admission of such documents. So to that extent I would be inclined to agree with you. But it depends on the way in which it is used and also whether there's any objection to admission to evidence of such a statement. And we just don't know at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, if -- I'll try it in a different way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know about the Council of National Resistance which, I think there's no dispute about this, existed in 1990 in the Krajina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes. After an attempted incursion into Benkovac, Obrovac, and Knin, when Babic declared a state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What happened after Babic declared a state of war in relation to the Council of National Resistance?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: They withdrew to Golubic. There was some barracks or, rather, huts there that had stayed over after certain public works, and then they wanted to show how dangerous the situation was and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness repeat what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could you -- sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could you repeat what you just said, Mr. Bosnic, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Milan Babic declared a state of war. Certain members of the leadership withdrew to the huts in Golubic that had stayed over after voluntary labour projects there in Yugoslavia, and subsequently they changed locations in order to stress the serious nature of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Who changed locations? Which leadership changed locations?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Milan Babic, Martic. They were later joined by Pero Stikavac, Mandinic. I can't recall them all now. They were mostly persons from the Knin area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were they members of the Main Board of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Save for Martic, I believe they all were, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And how does this relate to the Council of National Resistance?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, we were talking about the Council of National Resistance, and you started off by saying Babic declared a state of war and then there was a retreat or withdrawal to Golubic.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What has that got to do with the Council of National Resistance?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Well, they withdrew to Golubic, the council headed by Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When was the Council of National Resistance formed and who was it formed by?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: This was Milan Babic's idea. It was set up at the point when Knin was exposed to a threat from an incursion of the Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In which point in time approximately?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: It was the 17th or the 18th of August, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How many people were in the Council of National Resistance?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: A dozen, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What was its stated purpose?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: To mount resistance in the event that the Croatian forces launch an attack on Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I'm looking at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I can leave it there and pick it up after the break, with Your Honours' leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll have a break, and we resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we proceed: Mr. Jordash, any answer to D56?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, the answer is the same as that we gave for D55, which is that Dragisa Ristivojevic, who was an assistant to Mr. Stanisic, gave the document to Mr. Stanisic in 1992. We -- yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my understanding was that this was going to be a document that we were going -- that the Defence was going -- one of the several documents that the Defence was going to submit an RFA to try to get the original version. Perhaps I'm mistaken, I do believe this is -- D55 and D56 were among that pile.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's right. And we did make a request to the National Council and so far we've heard nothing back interest them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When did you make that request?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: 6th of October, 2010.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And have you insisted on receiving an answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, we've insisted on receiving an answer to many things, and we intend to make it part of a soon-to-be-filed motion asking Your Honours to intervene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Don't hesitate to seek the support of the Chamber in obtaining documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, we've certainly reached that point where we will be filing something forthwith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, I do not intend to spend a lot of time on it at this moment, but.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: This is a different matter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Different matter, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I just wanted to raise for Your Honours the fact that we have just today received a response to an RFA we sent to the Republic of Croatia. We sent it immediately upon receipt of the Defence witness list. We received now back today an 85 -- 85 pages in response to Mr. Bosnic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Today you received it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Today we received it. Now, I cannot express our position on it. It's in B/C/S, it's in Cyrillic also, so it takes some time for that to be reviewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: We will -- we're reviewing it with the utmost of urgency. I just wanted to let Your Honours know that that was the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You would say if it would be in Roman script it would be far easier for you, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: There are some people who can do better with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, that's the easiest thing to do is to read the Cyrillic letters, but then to understand the language. Mr. Jordash, a totally different matter: I asked you specifically before the break whether a B/C/S version of the proofing notes did exist because I thought it might be useful to have that available for the witness to -- now, you said no, but I do understand, unless it was produced in 20 minutes, but I take it that it was there because it has been shown to me over the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, it was produced during the court proceedings by our assistant who fortunately works very fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If she started translating it when I asked the question and when it was finished by then, I must praise her for the speed in which she is able to put, I take it, provisional translations on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, she saved us on many an occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's great to hear. I do also understand that it has been provided to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think that's right. And if I then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you can proceed on the basis of that. Has it been uploaded yet or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, it has on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If I can take the witness straight to that now and deal with that formality.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Bosnic, we want to just return to the amendments. So I want to deal with formalities before we return back to the substance of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Please could we have on e-court D314. Sorry, on the screen, I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: On the 8th of July, Mr. Bosnic, did you review your statement and make amendments to it?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If we could go to the bottom of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you recognise these amendments?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do these amendments reflect the clarifications you wanted to make at that time to your statement?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes, except for paragraph 3, right at the start.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And would you want to make a clarification to that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes. The word "accepted" has been left out. However, after the first round of multi-party elections, the leaders of the SDP left the -- abandoned the SDP programme and accepted Tudjman's idea. The word "accepted" is not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Apart from that, do these amendments reflect what you wanted to say and what clarifications you wanted to make?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes. I looked at it over the break and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the statement plus these amendments are, in substance, what you would answer if asked the same questions today?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And those answers are in accordance with the truth?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: I took an oath, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May the statement and the amendments be tendered, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D313 and D314 are admitted into evidence. Mr. Jordash, one final comment: The map marked by the witness, I already complained about the time it took, but if you look at it now, where it's totally unclear what was marked by the witness when, upon what question. It looks like a Rorschach test at this moment rather than anything else. Of course, sometimes you can read on the map what it is but often it's just dots. And since we are not psychiatrists but lawyers and we do not interpret Rorschach tests, the Chamber would not oppose an agreed map with the relevant markings with understandable -- not only for us but also if at any later stage anyone would have to look at it such as the Appeals Chamber, then of course it's totally useless as it is now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We'll arrange a map then and have the Prosecution look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, one of the things that still has to be done is that - to D314, which are the proofing notes - that the B/C/S translation should attach -- be attached to it, because if I open my e-court, it is -- and, as a matter of fact, you can't do that, but the Registry is the only one who can do it. So if it is ready to be attached, I'll instruct the Registrar to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, you are hereby instructed to attach the uploaded translation of D314, proofing notes, and make it part of D314. Everything's now on the record. Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Bosnic, are your headphones comfortable? You look as though you're constantly struggling with them and it's making me nervous.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: It's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. The Council of National Resistance - let's just try to move through this swiftly - what was its purpose, what did it do?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Its purpose was to co-ordinate the activities of village guards and the police in the event that the Croatian forces of the Croatian Special Police units advance into this particular area of Lika, Northern Dalmatia, and specifically Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What was it anticipating that the Special Police units of the Croatians would do upon advance?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: What was anticipated was crimes and civilian victims. It was expected that they wanted to enter the area in order to destroy the Serbian people there and place the territory under Croatian control.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How long did the Council of National Resistance exist?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: For a very short period of time. A month or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How did it dissolve or how was it disbanded?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Well, it simply ceased to operate. What was embarked upon was an effort to institutionalise Lika and the entire area into a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What did that mean in a practical sense, to institutionalise Lika and the entire area into a whole?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: This means that institutions would be set up, such as the TO, a proper police force, a secretariat for health care, a secretariat for education, et cetera, in order to create counterparts, as it were, to these same institutions in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Let's return, if I may, to the statement of Mr. Ognjen, which is D302. You've read this statement. Could you just assist in this regard: Biserko Ognjen, son of the father Ilija, do you know what his ethnicity was? Can you tell by his name?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: It's very hard to tell, but I do assume he's a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, reading the statement - you've read the statement, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And it lists a number of people, on page 1 of the English and 1 of the B/C/S and 2 of the English and 2 of the B/C/S, who were members of the Council of National Resistance. If you want to, you can remind yourself. But the question is: Do you agree with that or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This is the exact example of what I was opposing before. Counsel can ask the witness who were members of the Council of National Resistance but not put to the witness a proposition directly from a statement like this and ask the witness to -- I mean, it's leading in the ultimate example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is leading, Ms. Marcus. The question, however, is to what extent that should be inadmissible at this moment. Would you know by heart who the members were, witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't be able to tell you all, but there was Mandinic, Vitas, Babic, Martic. There were others. I can't give you the names of all of them. There were more of them for sure, but I can't recall all their names. It was a long time ago. You'll understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not know how important is it for you, but if Mr. Jordash would like to refresh the memory of the witness then he is allowed to do so. Ms. Marcus, to some extent I do agree with you that of course it's leading, but in a Tribunal where proofing witnesses, showing whatever you want to show to them before you examine them in chief, and then to say you shouldn't lead is, of course, well, a bit inconsistent from a systematic point of view, because then it's not a long-term memory but rather the short-term memory of whether he remembers what he saw yesterday. So to that extent let's try to remain practical as well. Mr. Jordash, if it's important for you, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well -- sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it's even a matter -- I do not know to what extent this would be matters on which one could even agree. I don't know what the formal status -- how formal it is and whether -- how many dispute there is about membership of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, let me deal with it in a different way, if I may, to shortcut things.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's been suggested by a witness in this court or a witness relied upon by the Prosecution that the Council of National Resistance was headed by Stanisic, Jovica Stanisic. Could you comment on that, please?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: That's nonsensical. No, that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Why do you say nonsensical?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Because I can't believe that this person could have stated something like that. It was simply not the truth. And anyone who was present in the area was aware of it. Everyone knew who the members were, at least the main ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you ever speak to Babic about this council?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: We discussed it in passing. But I talked about it from other -- I talked about it with other individuals from the SDS who were knowledgeable about these matters, and one of them, Petar Stikavac, is mentioned in this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What was your relationship to Petar Stikavac?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: We were on excellent terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Professionally or personally?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Initially professionally and later on personally because Petar was one of the founders of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And we're talking about a period in 1990; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Beginning, middle, or end of 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Our professional relationship began sometime in May and our friendship in mid-1991. The professional relationship dates back to May 1990 and our friendship from mid-1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, looking at this statement on the screen, at the beginning there's a reference there to the "state of war being declared in Knin on the 17th of August, 1990, by Knin SAO president Milan Babic for the purpose of defence from special units of the Republic of Croatia which had tried in the previous evening to confiscate some weapons from the Benkovac and Obrovac public security police stations." Now, in relation to the attempt by -- or the purported attempt, according to this statement, of the special units of the Republic of Croatia to seize weapons, was that something you observed or experienced in Croatia at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: I was not in Knin at the time. And these events took place in Dalmatia. And what I know comes from the meetings discussing these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, at paragraph -- let's return to your statement. Paragraph D313, paragraph 4, you note at the bottom, halfway through the paragraph, in relation to the night guards: "The people guarding were civilian inhabitants of the villages and were carrying their own licensed hunting arms. We informed the police stations in our municipalities, who still were in contact with Zagreb and not with Knin, that we were not going to allow," and here's an amendment, "the Croatian police to take out the armament of reserve forces and bring the armament in the Karlovac and Zagreb police stations." Do you recall giving that evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What were the reserve forces that you refer to, reserve armament?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: This was part of the police force in the municipalities of Vojnic and Vrginmost.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What were the -- did this have anything to do with weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: No. The weapons were kept under key, and by establishment they belonged to the reserve police force and could only be used in the event of a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did the police stations all have reserve weapons at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Croatia and elsewhere throughout Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What kind of reserve weapons did the police stations have?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: They had automatic rifles, gas masks, and that was it, so automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what kind of amount, volumes, of reserve weapons did the police stations have?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: They were small quantities. The reserve force had approximately -- the strength of the reserve force was approximately the same as the peacetime force in regular conditions. Of course, it depended on the actual area in question covered by the specific police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know what the reserve weapon volume was for Knin before Martic took over the station?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: No, but the principle was the same everywhere. The weapons had been there for -- from before, for some ten years or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's move on to paragraph 9 of your statement and the barricades that went up in Knin. Were these organised by anyone?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: The barricades went up spontaneously in response to threats and the attempts of the Croatian police forces to come to the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And after arising spontaneously, were they organised subsequently?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes. Barricades were also erected in the area of Lika, in municipalities where the SDS had power, having won [indiscernible] the elections; whereas in Kordun and Banija, this started only later. In fact, they only had night watches, they did not have barricades. Night guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to visit or pass through the barricades?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes. Every time we came to Knin, we had to pass by the barricades.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was there anybody manning the barricades who were not locals?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: To my knowledge, no, these were people in their ordinary clothes which they normally wore at home and with just hunting rifle -- armaments.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What role was Martic playing at this point in time, the time when the barricades went up?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: At that time Martic was a police inspector in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was he attending any SDS meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: No, he was not. At least not the Main Board meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you observe what his relationship was with Milan Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: They were on quite good terms, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's move forward now to 1991. You've told us that you were meeting Babic during this period. At what point was the government of Krajina formed?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: It was formed when the 7th municipality from that area, which is Vojnic from Kordun, accepted the Statute of the SAO Krajina. I cannot recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How was the government formed, can you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Following a proposal by Milan Babic at a session of the Main Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And how was it implemented, the suggestion or proposal?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: This proposal was accepted by the Assembly of the SAO Krajina, which was composed of seven MPs from each of the municipalities from the area of the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the Assembly of the SAO Krajina, how were the decisions made in the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: The proposal of the Main Board of the SDS, Milan Babic would refer it to the government. Actually, the government's proposal would be proposed to the Assembly by him, which would then take a vote. Actually, the creator of that policy was Milan Babic, at that time already man number one in the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you have a role to play in the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Only as of November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Up until that time were you in contact with members of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes. And when the preparations for the Assembly were underway, I would refer to the Vojnic delegates, the stances of the SDS, either decisions that they would be voted on, and I acquainted them with these decisions, so, rather, the proposals of decisions that they would be voting on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's just break that down a little. You would refer to the Vojnic delegates, stances of the SDS. Could you just explain that a little?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: That is the principle of work. That is how we worked prior -- in every municipality. Namely, an SDS -- the SDS representative and the delegation would acquaint the delegation which comprised seven delegates with all the materials which were discussed at the Main Board session of the SDS, which would then be part of the Assembly agenda so that at the Assembly session they would vote on any proposed decisions in keeping with the discussions at the Main Board and their stance taken there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have P1119, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This is a decision to appoint Milan Martic as secretary of the interior of the Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina, issued by the Executive Council of the Serbian Autonomous District Krajina in Knin, signed by Milan Babic, 4th of January, 1991. It's in the chart at number 2. You say in the chart: "I was present when the SDS Main Board discussed and adopted this decision. Milan Babic recommend Milan Martic." Who else was present at the SDS Main Board when this was discussed?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: There were over a hundred people present. I'm not sure of the exact number. Over a hundred members of the Main Board from the entire area of the SAO Krajina, Western Slavonia and Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know or were you given any reasons why Babic recommended Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Milan Babic recommended him, explaining that he was the first to adopt the initiative of the people not to allow their weapons to be seized and who placed himself at the helm of the resistance of the police to such a decision.
