He said that he was a man from Knin, that he was well known for being a patriot and a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You make the comment in your chart that the Executive Council adopted the recommendation afterwards and appointed Milan Martic. How was the decision made at the Executive Council to adopt the recommendation?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Milan Babic, as the president of the Executive Council of the Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina, with a party leadership and other members of the council who were the presidents of the municipalities proposed this decision, the council adopted that decision, and Milan Babic signed the adopted decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How was the decision adopted? Was it put to the vote?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. And it had to be adopted by a majority. And as far as I know, this particular decision was accepted, adopted, unanimously.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Would counsel please switch off his microphone while the witness is responding. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: During that decision-making process, did you hear of Jovica Stanisic? Did Stanisic have anything to do with that decision from where you were able to observe?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, and I believe that I was very familiar with matters, Jovica Stanisic had nothing whatsoever to do with the adoption of that decision. Had he had anything to do with that decision, I certainly would have known that and the others would have been informed. Milan Babic never mentioned Jovica Stanisic or anybody else in connection with this decision. That had been exclusively a proposal of his.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we have, please, P1907. In Your Honours' chart, page 2, number 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, if I -- if you allow me to interrupt you for a second. You earlier referred to a witness or at least a statement on which the Prosecution relied in relation to the -- who chaired the -- I have difficulties in finding it. I'd like to re-read exactly what that evidence is. Do you have any source for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This is the witness who claimed that Stanisic was in control of the Council of National Resistance, is that the issue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's the issue, but I -- even with all my search engines, I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, it's Mr. Babic himself. And he refers to this on a number of occasions, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- for example, P1878, and it's page 339 on e-court, and it's evidence Babic gave on 26th of November in the Milosevic trial, page 13490, where Babic talked about trying to disband the Council of National Resistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll have a look at it. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: P1907, Mr. Witness, an unsigned document with the name of Milan Babic, regarding a decision to establish the Secretariat for the Interior of the Serbian Autonomous Region of Krajina, 4th of January, 1991. And you comment that Article 7 shows that Martic was not in charge of the internal organisation of the Secretariat, but it was Milan Babic through the Executive Council. Could you just elaborate on that a little, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: As regards the internal organisation of the work of the Secretariat, this could not have been decided by Martic alone. It had to be decided by the council or, rather, the Executive Council of the SAO Krajina. The internal organisation and the actual mode of operation of the Secretariat could not have been actually decided upon by Martic but had to be adopted by the council as an organ, not by Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did Martic play any role in this?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He participated in the preparations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did he have a vote on the Executive Council?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Only after his appointment as secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How do you have this information? How do you know this?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: I know on the basis of the work of the Main Board. We know how the Executive Council of the Serbian Autonomous District functioned, and we know how they adopted decisions. Members of the board, all of them except for Martic, I believe, were members of the council. I apologise, of the main SDS board.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know if this decision or this establishment of the Secretariat had anything to do with Serbia and particularly Jovica Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. Namely, Milan Babic never mentioned Jovica Stanisic in connection with the proposal of this decision or in connection with the proposal to appoint Milan Martic as secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know at this time how often Martic and Babic were associating and the nature of that association?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: I believe that they co-operated on a daily basis. Namely, they agreed on activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have, please, the chart on the screen, D315.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And I want to ask you about a comment you made in the chart. It's page 2 of the chart, and it's in relation to Exhibit P1101. And at page 2 of the exhibit or the chart, having looked at an order to mobilise the Territorial Defence of the Serbian Autonomous District Krajina and volunteer units in order to defend citizens and its territorial integrity issued by Dr. Milan Babic, president of the Executive Council of the SAO Krajina, 1st of April, and you note: This document confirms my knowledge that it was Babic who issued orders to Martic and others in relation to the mobilisation of the TO. What knowledge do you have of that relationship other than that document?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: This document was in fact a request to the Government of Serbia and the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia because it was high time they helped us in technical terms and by training in order for us to set up a unit that would be prepared and able to resist Croatian special units, because their raid in Plitvice definitely proved that our village guards and regular police were simply not able enough in military terms to counter such incursions of the Croatian special units or of the units of the Croatian National Guards Corps. And we had nobody else to turn to but the Government of Serbia and the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You make the point there in the comments that Babic told you in 1992 that he had good relations with Bogdanovic in 1991. Can you recall the conversation and what was said?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes, Babic told me that he had good relations with Bogdanovic and that he had addressed him as well and met with him when he arrived in Belgrade. And that those were really good relations was confirmed by Bogdanovic himself because we met at a meeting in Belgrade in 1992 when Babic asked Bogdanovic to help iron out the Babic/Milosevic relationship. I too attended that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: P1892, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This is an order --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This is on, Your Honours, page 3 of the chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: An order issued by Milan Babic, president of the Serbian Autonomous District Krajina government, a minister of defence to mobilise all Territorial Defence headquarters and units on the territory, the Serbian Autonomous District Krajina. And in the chart you make the comment that this document again shows that Milan Babic was in charge of the mobilisation of the TO of Krajina. Could you explain what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Well, you can see here that Milan Babic is signing as the minister of defence and the prime minister, so he had a dual function in order to be able to keep tabs on things. It was he who issued orders. He personally issued orders to Territorial Defence staffs in the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, what did it mean in practical terms at that point in time for Milan Babic to be signing as the minister of defence? What power did he have as minister of defence?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: He had powers to order mobilisation of the Territorial Defence; for lists to be drawn up of men comprised within the Territorial Defence, to see what their particular skills were, their digits within the military establishment, whether they would belong to the infantry or the artillery branch; what was lacking, what was the strength of the able-bodied population in the area covered by a specific Territorial Defence staff, i.e., within a specific municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And at that point in time what Territorial Defence unit existed? We're talking about middle of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: There was a TO unit in every municipality. And its strength, of course, depended on the particular municipality, on the numbers of the population of a specific municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can you give some examples?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: For instance, in the area of Vojnic, it was the strength of a brigade, between 1600 and 1800 people. But I apologise, I think it is of the essence to say that the TO was under JNA command.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And how was it armed? Where did the TO unit receive their arms?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: TO units had some personal weapons which was also stored in warehouses. And as for the rest, it would be given to them by the JNA in time of war, in the event of war, and the JNA would be deciding on the manner of use of all Territorial Defence units in any areas where military operations were taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, you say Babic had powers to order the mobilisation of the Territorial Defence. How would that process take place? Did he make the decision himself or was it subject to agreement? How did it happen in practical terms?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: I believe that Babic could not sign such a decision without the agreement of the federal Secretariat for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was this subject to any government decision within the Krajina or not?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: In actual terms not, but formally, yes, in order to demonstrate that the Krajina could function autonomously.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you speak to Babic about his function as minister of defence?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: No. I considered it normal because that was the adopted staffing scheme, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about allegations made by Babic. And Babic makes various allegations about a parallel structure. Do you know anything about a parallel structure which removed power from Babic in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: No. I received my powers in late 1991 personally from Milan Babic. It was only at a later date that this was passed through the Assembly of SAO Krajina when I was appointed president of the War Presidency for the municipality of Slunj.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You received your powers in late 1991. Which powers were these, which position did you receive personally from Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: I was a representative of the civilian authorities for the municipality of Slunj. I was charged with creating all the necessary conditions for the civilian authority in Slunj to function normally; that means health care, schools, police, postal services, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How was Babic able to give you that position?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: By virtue of him being the prime minister. The decision had been taken previously to set up civilian authorities in Slunj, stationed in Veljun, but this had never taken hold. Now, once the Croatian population abandoned Slunj and Slunj was emptied, Babic said, Where is the civilian government there? He was told that there was none. At that point he called me and told me, Bosnic, it is your task now to set up civilian authorities in Slunj and you will be the president of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know if Babic acted in that way only in relation to you or was he making other appointments?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: I am familiar with this case which involved myself. The situation in Slunj was somewhat peculiar compared to the other municipalities in SAO Krajina. But I do know that he was the one who suggested that Milan Martic appoint specific chiefs of police stations in Kordun. In that context, I suggested who should be the chief of police for the municipality of Slunj to Milan Babic; that was Milos Pajic. I -- and as for Martic's assistants for Kordun, that was supposed to be Toso Pajic. Those were my proposals that I submitted to Milan Babic at his request. He in turn forwarded them to Martic, and Martic appointed both of them, complying with his request.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Let's just break that down a little. At what point in time are you referring? When did Babic make the proposal for Toso Pajic to be appointed?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: It was sometime in early December. Milan Babic told me that Martic had asked him to ask me if there was good policemen whom Martic could appoint as his assistant charged with the area of Kordun. I applied first to Milos Pajic who was in Slunj. He told me that there was someone better than him, namely Toso Pajic. This is what I conveyed to Milan Babic. And Milan Martic, in February of 1992, appointed Pajic as his assistant for Kordun.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: as his deputy for Kordun.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about some allegations that Babic made.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: P1878, e-court page 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And I want you to comment on some allegations. At transcript 18th of November, 2002, Babic testified in the Milosevic trial about a so-called parallel structure in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Page reference: 46.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And Babic asked -- is asked: "What do you mean when you say 'so-called parallel structure in the Krajina'?" "A. I mean by this a group of people which consisted of members of the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia, Public Security Service of Serbia, people from the police in the Serbian municipalities in Croatia, and other people who were in close contact with them and which had not been established by the legal authorities in Krajina or Croatia or Serbia ... which played a special role in all the events starting from August 1990 and in the following years. "Q. Who was in this -- in the centre from the personality? Who was in the centre of this parallel structure? "A. The central figure was the chief of the State Security Service of Serbia, Jovica Stanisic, followed by his assistant, Franko Simatovic, then Captain Dragan 'Rasko' Vasiljkovic, and other people from the State Security ... Serbia. Also Milan Martic from the police force in Knin, several other people from the police force, and many other people later. "In fact, later, it was the entire police force in Serbian municipalities Orlovic, Vitas; and presidents of the municipalities who were closely related to them, Bozovic, Rastovic, Benkovac, Zecevic, and other people." Could you provide your comment on that allegation, please -- or those allegations. First of all, did you observe during your political and social activities members of the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia making and acting -- sorry, did you observe members of the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia making decisions which impacted upon the Government of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: I would have been offended had someone taken decisions on my behalf. I would have considered myself useless. There were few of us and we knew one another well. The story of someone being here who was from Serbia is ridiculous. It could not have happened without our knowledge. I did my job in accordance with the law. I didn't know of any parallel organs, nor did they exist in Kordun. I had never heard of anything like that, and it's simply not the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Babic makes the point about later on this parallel structure consisting of "the entire police force in the Serbian municipalities Orlovic, Vitas; and presidents of the municipalities who were closely related to them, Bozovic, Rastovic, Benkovac, Zecevic, and other people." What was Babic's relationship with Orlovic during 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, the relationship was fair. And Babic was at loggerheads with presidents of these various municipalities who were founders of the SDS. I suppose they were unhappy with their status, and they used political means to counter certain positions expressed by Babic. But all these positions that Babic advocated were in fact pushed through, and Babic's proposal for the establishment of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina was in fact carried. On the 29th of December, 1991, it was, indeed, established. Whereas all these other individuals you mentioned, Bozovic and others, fought against it. It was on the 19th of December, not the 29th.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. So just slow down a minute.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What was the nature of their dispute and how did it manifest itself?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: It manifested itself in political disagreements. They believed that they were due a larger share of power and that they should have some say-so in the decision-making process, but this was merely a verbal confrontation at meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What kind of meetings were they engaged in?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: These were party meetings and Assembly sessions. And I mean the Assembly of SAO Krajina, later the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you present at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: I was present at party meetings from the start, and I started attending Assembly sessions in late November 1991. I would meet all these various individuals. I first saw Mr. Jovica Stanisic in 1994. As for Mr. Simatovic, I saw him in person for the first time here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Going back to the political dispute about the establishment of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, please explain how that dispute took place and what happened. How was it that Babic succeeded against that opposition?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Generally our political position was to follow all or nearly any activities undertaken by Croatia. If Croatia wanted to secede, we would be asking to secede from Croatia the day before. If Croatia wanted to strip us of our constituent status, then we wanted to be the first ones to secede from Croatia. If a referendum was discussed, we wanted to be the first ones to call a referendum. Babic believed that we had to proclaim the Serbian Republic of the Krajina in order that we too, as Croatia, may ask for our rights to be recognised and as well as secession. This was where the conflict stemmed from. Milan Babic went to Belgrade for discussions with Slobodan Milosevic. While in Belgrade, he placed a call to the party head office asking that an Assembly be convened, which was supposed to be the constituent Assembly of the Serbian Republic of the Krajina. On the evening before the Assembly session, he convened the Main Board and said that this was the only way for us to counter Croatia. We accepted his arguments and the Assembly was scheduled for the 19th. Even though the Main Board members were opposed to the idea, they went along with it at the very session and that was how the RSK was proclaim. Later on, Babic said that Slobodan Milosevic was opposed to the idea of proclaiming the RSK. I asked him, How was that possible? Well, Babic said -- on my way out of his office, I told him that we would not be proclaiming the republic, but as I got into the car, I said to myself, What do I care? We are going ahead with it anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And during the Assembly meeting where this was decided, was this decided by a vote?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was there discussion in the Assembly concerning Milosevic's view?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: No, we weren't aware of Milosevic's view at all. This was something that Babic told me at a later date. We accepted the proposed decision by acclimation. All the deputies in attendance, and every municipality had seven delegates, and I mean all the municipalities of Krajina, and that's how the RSK was proclaimed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And these presidents of the municipalities who'd disagreed with the proposal, how was their relationship with Babic following this disagreement?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: They complied with decisions of the parliament. They stayed in their positions as members of parliament. Rastovic was in Lapac. Bozovic was in Korenica. I think they were each in charge of the various municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's change subjects slightly and go to Exhibit 5595. These are -- or this is a diary written by Mladic. I want to ask you about some military matters which Mladic discusses.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And page 52 of the English and the B/C/S. I've been told that it's the break time, although I'm not sure of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's approximately break time, yes. If this would be a suitable moment, we would take the break now and we would resume at quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, before we continue, could you give us an estimate because we never received an 92 ter estimate as the time remaining for the examination of the witness. Initially for viva voce I think it was four to five hours. Could you give us --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I still wanted to take between four and four and a half hours. As Your Honours know, we dropped a witness who is going to be dealing with the Krajina and therefore I wanted to take a little bit longer with this witness to deal with some aspects of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll see. Please try to avoid repetitions from what is already on paper. That's what sometimes happens. Further, I would like to remind you that if a witness testifies under Rule 92 ter in open court, that you are supposed, as a matter of fact already at the beginning, to read a summary so as to inform the public about what your follow-up questions, what they do follow up at.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That you might have forgotten that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We did, yes. I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move on. And please keep in mind that is important for the public character of the trial. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Before we turn to this diary, I just want to ask you about, just very briefly, about Milan Babic's various titles, and I don't think there's going to be a dispute, so I'll lead unless there's objection. Milan Babic in 1990 was the president of the municipal committee of the SDS in Knin; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And in the same year, he was president of the Knin Municipal Assembly; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And in the same year, he was president of the temporary presidency of the community of Northern Dalmatia and Lika municipalities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And in the same year, he was president of the Serbian National Council; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And in the same year, he was president of the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And in the same year, he was president of the temporary Executive Council of the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And in 1991 he was a member of the regional committee of the SDS Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And in the same year, he was president of the Executive Council of the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And in 1991, same year, he was president of the Government of the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And in the same year, he was the commander of the TO of the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And in the same year, he was the defence minister in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And in the same year, he was the commander of the SAO Krajina Armed Forces?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you able, just very briefly, to give an insight into how one man managed to accumulate so many titles?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Well, admittedly not all of these functions were held at the same time. But at any given time, Babic had several title. We trusted him and we thought it best for him to occupy some of the key positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And during 1990 and 1991, were those positions given to him by vote?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were there those within the various bodies, from the National Council to the Executive Council to the government, who opposed his election?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: For the most part, no, unless there was a personal confrontation like in the case of the presidents of the municipalities of Korenica and Lapac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's turn to the Mladic diaries. And 65 ter 5595 and page 24, which is on the screen. And it relates to entry on the 1st of July, 1991. Now, were you familiar, in your political role, with military events on the ground during 1991? Did you receive information about the role of the army and the role of Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: About the role of the army, yes. And Mladic was mentioned both in the areas of Dalmatia and Kordun, where I personally participated in communications, meetings, discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What was the source of your information, in the main?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: For the general picture, it was Mr. Milan Babic and other persons I met within Knin. As for Kordun, they were members of the police, representatives of the zone staff of the Territorial Defence with whom we as representatives of either the party or the civilian authorities would communicate. And some of them we even nominated for appointment within the TO, where they were appointed by Babic. And finally, the TO was part of the army, and it was in that context that we also learned of the various issues concerning the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Would you attend meetings which concerned the role of the TO in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What kind of meetings were they?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: They dealt with the way in which the TO was supposed to be set up and operate, because Babic was not successful in having a unified system of the TO up and running across Krajina in terms of all the TO commanders who were appointed, being his own men, men loyal to him and the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So how did that fact become part of the meetings? Who was meeting, and in what circumstances, concerning the unification of the TO?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: There was a meeting of the Main Board, and later just we from the area of Kordun remained with Babic. There was me and another three people from Banija. There was Mile Paspalj, who later was the president of the Assembly of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina. The problem arose in connection with a fact, that the TO in the area of Kordun, the municipal TO of Kordun, Vojnic, and Vrginmost, accepted Mile Dakic whom Mile Babic had appointed commander of the TO. So the discussion was about how to overcome the situation. And Milan Babic said then that the best thing to do would be for him to consult his contacts within the federal Secretariat of National Defence in Belgrade, and following an agreement with them in respect of the zone staffs, we should appoint retired officers who hailed from Krajina and were now retired and lived in Serbia. In fact, we accepted this idea of his, and shortly thereafter new appointments were made and staffs were established, appointed by Milan Babic, which started functioning throughout the Krajina area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's break that down a little. When did these events you've just described take place?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: This took place in 1991. Now, was it March or May? I cannot be sure now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What was Babic's principal complaint?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Babic's principal complaint was that the personnel that he wished to have replaced were people from the communist era and that they were perhaps also co-operating with the Croats and that that should be changed. But because of the resistance --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me take this step by step, please. Babic wanted to replace which personnel?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: The TO staff commanders in the areas of Kordun and Banija municipalities, which later accepted to join the SAO Krajina, those municipalities, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Why did he want to replace the TO staff commanders in Kordun and Banija municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: In order to appoint his people, his party, people who were suitable for him, who suited him not only according to the party line but also in other ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Who had selected the TO staff commanders in Kordun and Banija, the ones he wanted to replace?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Well, they were there in the earlier system, the so-called system of national defence at the level of Yugoslavia. These people specifically had been appointed by the TO staff of Croatia at the time while Yugoslavia still was a single state.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What action did he take to try to replace the TO staff commanders?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: He issued orders on the replacement of these people and orders on reappointments, on appointments.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Who did he issue orders to?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: He issued these orders to the municipal TO staffs for the replacement of so and so - I cannot recall the exact names at this point - and for so and so to be installed in that person's stead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And was the order followed?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: On what basis was there a refusal to follow the order?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: People at the local level were of the view that the proposed people were not, A, competent, and, B, that that he did not have the necessary authority in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What happened when they refused to follow the order?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Babic looked for another solution and he came up with the idea that zone staffs should be established and that he should discuss with the federal Secretariat of National Defence in Belgrade the actual names and agree on them, that they should be professionals, that they should hail from the area of Krajina. And for the most part these were retired JNA officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did he discuss with members of the federal Secretariat of National Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. He actually brought back ready-made solutions. He signed the order on their appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know who he spoke to in the federal Secretariat of National Defence, who he was co-operating with?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: I believe that his name was Jokic. I'm not quite certain. It is Jokic with a J. And there were quite a few other names that I cannot recall at this moment, but I do know that the address was federal Secretariat for National Defence, Admiral Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And how was this issue then resolved?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: These officers were appointed and they came and the zone staff was established first for Kordun and later for Kordun and Banija. And principally in the command structures of these staffs were men appointed by Babic at the proposal of the federal Secretariat for National Defence. And pursuant to an agreement with the federal Secretariat, they actually arrived in our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you in communication with Babic during this period over this event and over these circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Who did Babic blame at that time for the circumstances that transpired, the refusal of the local TO or local authorities to follow his order?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Well, the representatives of the local authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can you remember who they were?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Well, the president of the municipality, the president of the Executive Council of the municipality, the chief of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did he hold Martic responsible for any of these circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: No, he did not. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did he ever mention Stanisic or Simatovic or anyone from the Serbian DB?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Never, ever. On no occasion did he mention them. What he would say is these are those old Commies who forget that the communist era has passed, and they belong to the League of Communists - Movement for Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you in agreement with his views at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Well, I was, because what mattered to me was that those people should be from Kordun. And they had high ranks, they were majors or colonels, and I thought that quite sufficient. But actually I did not personally know any of those people nor had I proposed them nor had any one of the people that I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's return or let's start with the Mladic diary. And page 24, relating to July 1991. And in particular, the 1st of July, 1991. And Mladic notes that: "The army has a task and a holy duty to prevent a fratricidal war. We must be proud of the fact that not a single victim has fallen in the zone of the corps." At that time are you able to -- let me start that again. Putting yourself back into that time, taking your mind back to July 1991, do you know what view you held about the role of the army, the JNA, at that point? And I mean you as an individual.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: It was a cold and warm position, a lukewarm position. We expected the JNA to fulfill its mission, the raison d'être of the JNA, to protect the territory of Yugoslavia overall, including us in that Yugoslavia. But what bothered us was the fact that those officers still lived in the communist era. They still carried this five-pointed star, a symbol of that past failed system. And we did not want our members of our defence to wear the five-pointed star; we wanted them to take it off. So that it was lukewarm or, rather, cold and warm in that system. They had not kicked their old habits as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In July of 1991, what role did the JNA play in relation to the events in the regions you were politically active in?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: The JNA's task was, and initially it did that, to prevent the conflict. But it did not do much to disarm the already-existing paramilitary units in Croatia, but [indiscernible] our relations with it were correct, because the Territorial Defence in the event of armed conflicts failed under the competence of the JNA and was supposed to comply with the orders of the JNA. On one occasion reservists without arms went to Karlovac, called by the JNA, they were then intercepted at the Karlovac bridge and all were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You make the point that the JNA did not disarm the already-existing paramilitary units in Croatia. Did you and your political colleagues form a view as to whether the JNA was acting properly in relation to the Croatian paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: It was our view that the JNA was not acting, so to speak, aggressively enough in relation to the paramilitary units. While we, until July or so, had only hunting weapons, they had automatic weapons. And the JNA, the army was saying that they would disarm them, but they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have page 52, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: While that's being found: Do you know what Babic's view was concerning the role of the JNA in July of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: I believe that his view was shared with my own view and that of the majority of people, and I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could you repeat the last sentence of your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: I know that Milan Babic communicated, talked with, and consulted with Ratko Mladic, if that is what you meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did Babic communicate with you any of those conversations?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember right now. I think that once he talked about this quarrel that he had had with Mladic regarding emblems. And as I've already said, our people were practically allergic to the five-point star and because of that they would not respond to calls for mobilisation from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Page 52, Friday, the 12th of July, 1991. Mladic describes members of the "National Guard Corps passing through Lelas and entering the defence line in Kijevo" and noting that the "numerical strength of the members of the MUP corps is growing, women are seen in Kijevo," across the page, "along with unidentified men. This is going outside the framework of the agreement because three months ago there were 300 and now there are 700 inhabitants." Do you know what this reference relates to and do you have any information on it?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: This refers to the village of Kijevo, where there was set up a police station of exclusively Croats in an area where there hadn't been one before. This shows that the numbers increased, namely that there were continued provocations of Serbian villages. Because to pass through a Serbian village which was called, I believe, Civljane, you had to pass through Kijevo. This also -- there was also harassment and maltreatment and what have you, and that is why they were demands for the Kijevo unit to be disarmed. But instead of that, the strength was increased. Later there was even a parade, and Vladimir Seks, as vice-president of the Croatian Assembly, came in a helicopter to support them in that provocation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The entry goes on to say: "Problem of providing passage through Kijevo for workers on their way to work because members of the MUP can stop a bus and capture hostages. The same bus is also taken by members of the army and inhabitants of Cetina." Are you familiar with the events in Cetina?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Well, I heard general information, not by name. The Main Boards named that it was a major problem and that those people were being arrested and searched and harassed and that they were actually concerned and apprehensive because they had to go to work to Knin every day and in order to go to work they had to pass through Kijevo every day. So that this was a cause of major concern among the people throughout Dalmatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have page 64, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Page 64, as you'll see, relates to 15th of July, 1991, and Mladic writes, in the third paragraph: "That the JNA must ensure peaceful resolution of the crisis. In our zone we can expect the situation to worsen, particularly in and around Benkovac." Did you observe the role of the JNA at this point in time and was it consistent with Mladic's description or not?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Well, we expected them to behave in that way, but they did not always conduct themselves in the way he has written. We expected them to be more resolute in dealing with the situation, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What do you mean by that? In which way were they not resolute in dealing with the situation?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: They did not disarm the paramilitary units which later provoked much fiercer conflicts in which, in addition to JNA members, police members as well as civilians perished, both on the Croatian and the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were they acting on anyone's side at this point in time, July of 1991, from what you could observe?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: No. No, they were not on anyone's side. They were still maintaining a neutral posture.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just so that we're clear: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Because they were not taking any actions, irrespective of the provocations coming from the Croatian side which also involved wounded and dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have next, please, diary 5596.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: While that's being found, let me just pick up on something you've just said, Mr. Bosnic. "Because they were not talking any actions, irrespective of the provocations coming from the Croatian side which also involved wounded and dead." What were the nature of the provocations and where were they?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Well, during the night they would be intercepting people, searches, opening fire at the villages. As far as Kordun is concerned, there were attempts of the National Guard Corps patrolling through Serbian villages. And at the end of July, the first killings of Serbs -- of Serb civilians in Kordun also happened, so that the Serbs started leaving the city of Slunj, in which they up to that point tried to go on living. And because of that, Slunj became practically ethnically cleansed or clean city without Serbs. And not far from Slunj is a military testing ground where there was a JNA unit posted which reacted only in November when their electricity supply was cut and their movement hampered, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How many men, women, and children of Serbian ethnicity left Slunj?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Well, it is difficult to say now the exact number, but at a minimum 500 would be the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Where did they go?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: They went to the villages, Serbian villages, in the municipality of Slunj, such as Veljun, Perjasica, Primislje, Zecevaras [phoen], and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When was this departure of Serbs from Slunj?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: After the killings which took place. That was sometime in June, I believe late June or early July. I cannot be sure. I believe it was the beginning of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go to page 33 of this diary. And the entry we're going to look at was written -- or, sorry, related to the 29th of August, 1991. And it's a reference, as you can see, to an "agreement reached on the 28th of August, 1991, in Knin between the Knin corps commander, Mr. Krpina, president of the Crisis Staff for the Central and Northern Dalmatia, and the presidents of Drnis and Sibenik SO, signatories of the agreement, is accepted." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know anything about this agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: I do not know the specifics. I only know that an agreement, a truce, was signed. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know of the role of the JNA in relation to the agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the role of the JNA was that of mediator. They actually linked the two sides. They were the guarantor that the agreement would indeed be implemented. And that, in fact, was the principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And can we go to page 324, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: 324 is an entry which relates to the 10th of November, 1991. And perhaps if we go to the page before to get the context, 323. And Mladic, underneath the heading "Neso," speaks about Babic and Djujic, and notes that "the staff made a mistake and blocked the mobilisation." And then there's further text before we go over the page. We can see Mladic's view or I should say Mladic's writing, where he notes: "Djujic irritates things to have everything go to the JNA. I'm concerned that the five-pointed star of Babic does not later turn into a cockade." Are you able to cast any light on that entry?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: If this is Djujic who was chief of the TO in Babic's office, then this means that all the persons who are under the TO command should not go over to the JNA. Mladic, on the other hand, wanted everyone to be under the competence of the JNA because of his fears that Babic's five-pointed star may turn into a cockade and that the TO may turn against the JNA if they continue pressing us with the five-pointed star and the symbols that we wanted to abandon. We did not want a one-party Yugoslavia; we wanted a democratic, multi-party Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you privy to any conversations at this point in time that Mladic had with Babic, whether being there personally or having spoken to Babic or anyone else?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: I didn't attend the discussions that Babic had with Mladic. We only had certain indications as to what the reasons for the lack of trust were and what the relationship between Mladic and Babic was. At Kordun, I did attend, occasionally, meetings of the TO, where representatives of the JNA were in attendance as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did Mladic -- I beg your pardon. Did Babic speak to you about his view of Mladic and the JNA in November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Babic's view was that regardless of the objections we may have in respect of the JNA, we did not have anyone else to rely upon, and that this is what we should be guided by in our relations with the JNA, as a necessary evil.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You make mention there to Djujic being the "chief of the TO in Babic's office" and, it seems a decision, that "persons who are under the TO command should not go over to the JNA." Did this have anything to do with Babic?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Excuse me, could counsel please identify what he is referring to. You make mention -- sorry, could we just have the reference that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Page 73, line 4 to 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me repeat the question for you, Mr. Bosnic. You make mention to Djujic being the "chief of the TO in Babic's office" and, it seems a decision, that "persons who are under the TO should not go over to the JNA." Did this have anything to do with Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes. We believed that this was a way in which we would begin the process of setting up our own army, that is to say, the army of the Krajina. And that at that stage, and such was the law, we were subordinated to the JNA. We thought that we should abide by this situation, although there were people out in the field who were opposed. Here they mention one Cubrilo who had already set up a Chetnik unit near Gospic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When you say "we believed that this was a way in which we would begin the process of setting up our own army," who's we?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Milan Babic and the SDS leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did this have anything to do with Martic?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, it didn't. Under the law, in times of war the JNA is re-subordinated to the JNA, and in this case it would be to the Army of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The police is re-subordinated to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did Babic take any steps to fulfill this aim of having your own army?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: There was this one quite clumsy and failed attempt to set up the King Peter's Guard, I think that's how it was called, in Kninsko Kosovo, near Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was there a resolution to this apparent dispute between Mladic and Babic? Was Mladic able to subordinate the TO against Babic's wish?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout Krajina up until Vance's Plan, the TO units as well as all the police units were, before the commencement of military operations, subordinated to the JNA, in other words, to their command, complied with their orders, and implemented their plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did Babic ever make a contemporaneous complaint during this process suggesting that this had anything to do with Stanisic or the DB of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: I had known Mr. Babic for a long time and was in contact with him after the war. He had never mentioned to me any sort of pressure or any contacts he may have had with Mr. Jovica Stanisic nor did I ever see him with Jovica Stanisic. I would travel with him to Belgrade often, and I had never seen Jovica Stanisic before 1994 nor did he tell me that he had been with Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's return to your statement, if we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have D313 on the screen, please. Paragraph 73.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Paragraph 73, you note that: "Milan Babic was my friend but I cannot believe that he claimed something," and it's been amended to "he claimed something like that. We went through a lot together. But I can tell you what he said before going to The Hague. He was trying to get some assistance from the official authorities of Serbia as to how to approach The Hague but no one cared or made any suggestions." Did you have a conversation or a number of conversations with him about this?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes. Since Milan Babic was not on good terms with Savo Strbac from the Veritas documentation centre, it was Savo Strbac who informed me, it was still in English, that Babic was going to be indicted, that in fact he was in that indictment charged with a joint criminal enterprise. I went with that piece of information to Babic, who asked me what it was that he was supposed to do. I advised him to consult with the authorities in Serbia, which was something that other individuals, common friends, advised him to do. But none of the official organs of Serbia wanted to receive him and advise him on the future steps or tell him what was going to become of his family. He was disappointed and ultimately said, somewhat brazenly as well in disparaging terms, If I should be the one to fall, then let everyone follow me. Or, in fact, he said, If I am to sink into that mud pit, then let everyone else sink with me. This was the result of the fact that nobody wanted to help him in Serbia as to what sort of a defence he should mount. Ever since he said that, I never saw him again until he appeared in The Hague. I saw him on TV and reacted in writing to the statements he made there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go to paragraph 35 of your statement, and it concerns the creation of Golubic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask a question in between. You earlier said - I didn't fully understand that: "... from the ... documentation centre, it was ..." and then a word is missing "who informed me, it was still in English, that Babic was going to be indicted, that in fact ..." Could you give more -- a little bit more detail as to what you learned and how you learned it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received a phone call from Savo Strbac, the director of the Veritas documentation and information centre. I suppose that he obtained the document in The Hague because the document was still in English. And it became obvious, on the basis of this document, that Babic was in an indictment charged with joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you see that document? because you say it was still in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Savo Strbac made a copy and asked me to take it to Mr. Milan Babic because he was not on good terms with Babic, and I did as he asked me to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And was it then Mr. Strbac who told you what was in the document, or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Savo Strbac told me that Milan Babic was in that joint indictment and asked me if I wanted to be the one to take it to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, I want to just ask you a little about your knowledge of Golubic. In paragraph 35, you note that: "Somewhere at the end of the May or the beginning of June 1991, part of the youth volunteered to be sent to be trained in Knin." Which youth volunteered?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: This was Serbian youth. They were young men who manned village guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You note in the same paragraph that: "The young people from Kordun went to Golubic in late May of 1991 ..." "There were two groups who were sent from Kordun and Banija ." When the people from Kordun went to Golubic in late May of 1991, had Golubic opened at this point?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: I think that it had just opened at that point. Some of them joined the first group as soon as it was opened, and others followed in the second group. So throughout its existence there were two groups of people who went to Golubic for training from Kordun, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When did Golubic close?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: When the second round of training was completed. It was sometime in June or July, I'm not sure. It had to do with the conflict between Babic and Captain Dragan.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you able to say, just for clarification, how many groups were trained at Golubic and what kind of numbers of people were trained?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Well, if 30 people went there from Kordun in two groups, one of which had 20 of them, the other 10 or vice-versa, so I suppose if you look at the entire area of Krajina it might amount to some 200 or 300 people, but I can't give you the exact number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I'd like to seek one matter clarified. You are talking about volunteers. Now, that always confuses me a bit. Volunteers can, as far as I understand, be persons who make themselves available for a certain job, but sometimes reference to volunteers is also to persons who do something without being paid for it. Now, what kind of volunteers are we talking about? Are we talking about those who go somewhere without being paid for what they're doing or are we talking about those who voluntarily made themselves available but were remunerated for their activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time of departure, the issue of remuneration was not mentioned at all. They went voluntarily in order to undergo training and share their knowledge upon their return. Whether they were paid ultimately is not something that I know, but I don't think so. But the understanding was not that they would be paid upon completing their training.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And was the understanding that they would be paid for any follow-up activities after the training?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, none of them went there to begin with in order to be paid ultimately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether they finally were paid either for the training or for what they did after they were trained, you do not know; is that a correct understanding of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that they were not paid during their training. Whether they received something later on, I don't know. I know that when they returned, nobody had received any pecuniary remuneration during their training there. That's what I mean; they didn't receive money.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did they receive anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They received their uniforms, bearing the insignia "Milicija Krajina," "Krajina Police," and we called them "Martic's Police."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Those were active as members of the Martic's Police, were they usually paid for their activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the best of my knowledge, not in Kordun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you mean by "not in Kordun"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew these individuals and I can speak for them. I cannot speak to the other areas because I was not in contact with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When the recruits or those who had been trained in Golubic returned to Kordun, what did they do? What were their tasks or duties as?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Their tasks were to continue manning village guards and to train other young individuals, to train them the skills that they themselves had acquired. All the while, the police force which was operational in Kordun and Banija and which had still been in contact with Zagreb would be replaced by them. This did not happen because in late June or July the police from the municipalities of Kordun and Banija severed all ties with Zagreb and recognised Martic as the secretary as well as the police of the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know how long the men from Kordun were trained at Golubic? How long did the training last?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: 15 days, I believe. But I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know what they were trained to do during those 15 days or so?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: They were trained how to handle side-arms. They had fitness training. They were trained how to move about as a group and communicate with gestures rather than voices. They were told that this was the way legionaires were trained, this because they were trained by Captain Dragan.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just to be as clear as possible: What was it then that distinguished -- or what was it, in additional to those skills or the training received by the police generally -- let me start that again. What did they learn in addition to what was normal police training at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Simply how to use automatic weapons in combat and how to get by in combat. I don't think there was anything else that they were doing according to what they told me. I didn't attend the training.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the object and purpose of the training was what, as you understood it? What was it they were being trained for and for what purpose?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: To be the nucleus of the units that were supposed to be ready to stand up to the Croatian National Guard and the Croatian police. When the police in Kordun and Banija agreed to join Knin and to -- rather than Zagreb, they agreed to becoming scouts, reconnaissance units, for the Krajina units.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did Golubic open again after its closure in, when you think, June or July of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC
utterances.text: Yes. Golubic was re-opened in 1992, in September roughly. At any rate, in the second half of 1992 Golubic was opened as a police school for the training of ordinary policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 1557, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I am --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document is reported to me as not being in e-court, Mr. Jordash. I suggest that you take 14 hours to find it. And meanwhile --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because we have to adjourn for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are almost at three hours at this moment. So if you said you would need four to four and a half hours, could I then take it that you try to finish at the first break or might need a bit more?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think I can finish by the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By the first break. That would be appreciated. Meanwhile, Mr. Bosnic, I would like to instruct you, because we'll adjourn for the day, I'd like to instruct that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether that is testimony you have given today or whether that is testimony still to be given tomorrow or perhaps the day after tomorrow. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00. We adjourn. And we'll resume tomorrow morning, the 13th of July, at 9.00 in this same Courtroom II. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 13th day of July, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.
